content: St. John Ambulance (SJA) in Canada is a highly respected and globally recognized non-profit organization specializing in first aid training. It is the most successful organization of its kind worldwide. SJA Canada serves communities through various initiatives aimed at improving health, safety, and quality of life by providing training and community services. History St. John Ambulance was established in Canada in 1882. Under its banner, volunteers across the country carry out humanitarian services on behalf of the Most Venerable Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem. In 1897, the Dominion Council of Canada was formed in Ottawa to legitimize the operations of the St. John Ambulance Brigade in Canada. Around the same time, the Brigade began its activities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. By 1933, the Dominion Council evolved into the Commandery of Canada due to the growing demand for first aid services and training. In 1946, the Priory of Canada of the Most Venerable Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem was established to address two key needs: the expanding role of the St. John Ambulance Association and Brigade across Canada, and the necessity of transferring governance of the Order to Ottawa, Ontario, away from the Priory of England and the Islands. Training St. John Ambulance is a national leader in first aid training, setting the standard for first aid, CPR, and other life-saving skills. The organization is supported by a highly skilled network of medical and healthcare professionals. SJA also offers advanced-level courses, such as the Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) program in several provinces, and operates the Maritime School of Paramedicine in Nova Scotia. Volunteer Brigade The St. John Ambulance Volunteer Brigade consists of trained volunteers who provide first aid services at public events, support during emergencies or disasters, and youth programs that promote community service and personal development. Brigade members in Canada are trained to a high standard of first aid, including the Medical First Responder (MFR) program. In Nova Scotia, the term Brigade or Ambulance is no longer used; instead, volunteers are referred to as St. John Volunteer Medical Response to better reflect their role in the community. Across Canada, SJA has over 25,000 members in more than 300 communities, serving people of all ages. Therapy Dog Program Recognizing the isolation faced by individuals in hospitals, seniors' residences, and nursing homes, St. John Ambulance initiated the Therapy Dog Program in Peterborough, Ontario, which has since expanded nationwide. This program partners with hospitals, palliative care units, day care centers, senior residences, rest homes, special needs schools, and psychiatric hospitals, where individuals are often unable to have pets. The medical community acknowledges the therapeutic benefits of interacting with animals, such as reduced blood pressure, alleviated tension, and emotional comfort. Stroke patients may use their affected hand to pet a dog, Alzheimer’s patients often recall memories of their own pets, and individuals with mobility can enjoy walking a dog. Even completely paralyzed patients, such as those with multiple sclerosis, can find comfort in cuddling a small dog. The program involves weekly visits by volunteers and their dogs, fostering a bond between the client, the dog, and the volunteer. We Can Help Program St. John Ambulance offers the We Can Help program to elementary school students aged seven to ten. This program introduces children to basic first aid skills and injury prevention, ensuring they are equipped with essential safety knowledge. It is designed to empower children, who often bear significant responsibilities, with the tools to respond effectively in emergencies. Friends of the Emergency Room The Friends of the Emergency Room program involves volunteers who provide comfort and support to patients and their companions in the emergency department of the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Alberta. These volunteers are an integral part of the emergency room care team, offering emotional support and assistance to those in the waiting room. Youth Programs Youth members of SJA Canada play a vital role in the organization. The Proficiency Program allows youth to earn the Grand Prior’s Award and work towards the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award. Proficiencies are awarded for demonstrating knowledge in various subjects, both related and unrelated to the organization. The program is designed to meet the requirements of the Grand Prior’s Award and equip youth with valuable life skills. To achieve the Grand Prior’s Award, participants must complete six compulsory and six elective proficiency courses. Youth members also have opportunities to engage in community service and provide patient care at public events under the supervision of trained adult members. Disaster Planning and Aid In emergencies, SJA Canada is prepared to provide disaster relief and emergency services to affected areas. The specific procedures depend on local disaster management plans, but the Government of Canada officially recognizes SJA’s role in these efforts. Supplies, equipment, and personnel availability may vary, but SJA has a National Duty Officer system in place to mobilize additional resources and personnel to support local divisions when needed.
